uncited: This family of techniques converts 3D geometric data into voxel grids by projecting or transferring information into 2D image space (textures) before reconstructing the 3D volume.

Unlike direct 3D rasterization, these methods leverage the GPU's fixed-function rasterizer or image load/store operations on 2D textures to determine voxel occupancy, often trading memory bandwidth for computational simplicity.

They are distinguished from direct triangle rasterization by operating on pre-computed surface samples or 2D texture slices, ensuring connectivity or enabling real-time performance insensitive to scene complexity [S1, unofficial].
All methods in this family rely on the mapping of world-space coordinates to discrete voxel indices.
This formula is applied consistently across Position Map Voxelization, Billboard Voxelization, and Hardware-accelerated Surface Voxelization to map continuous geometry to the discrete 3D grid.
The concept of using image-space techniques for volume generation stems from the efficiency of GPU rasterization hardware.
By projecting 3D data into 2D textures, developers can utilize standard graphics pipeline stages for coverage testing and interpolation.
This approach is particularly prevalent in real-time applications such as video games and interactive simulations, where performance is critical.

The specific variants described here have been developed to address limitations in memory usage, connectivity, and scene complexity sensitivity, with origins in various unofficial graphics programming communities and technical blogs [S1, unofficial].
